newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican debt repayment seen helping market access.
newsitem.headline: Mexican debt repayment seen helping market access.

text.p: Mexico's early payment of its debts to the U.S. Treasury should help charge the country's energetic return to international financial markets, government officials said on Wednesday.
Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz told reporters Mexico's early repayment of some $3.5 billion to the U.S. Treasury will increase its access to international capital markets.

"From here on in, in the way that we are reducing the country risk and we are reprogamming and restructuring our maturing debt, we will have better conditions of access to international financial markets...," Ortiz said.
He added that the premium Mexico pays on its debt could be reduced as the amount of debt maturing falls.
The announcement of the prepayment gave an immediate boost to Mexico's financial markets, which may have been at least part of what was behind the early morning announcement, analysts said.

"What they are doing is making a positive impact on financial markets. They choose this moment because they want to keep the good movements in financial markets," said ING Barings economist Sergio Martin.
Helping rehabilitate Mexico in the eyes of the United States could also be part of the agenda.
"What Mexico wants to show is that you can trust us, that we make a few mistakes, but in the end we payback our debts," Martin said.

The market seems to agree. The spread that Mexico pays on its debt issue has been narrowing against U.S. Treasuries and demand has remained strong, with the latest placement being a $1.0 billion 10-year global issue last week.
Mexican officials also suggested the country could make an early repayment of some of the huge debts it still owes the International Monetary Fund.

Those funds, plus the funds received from the U.S. government, helped keep Mexico afloat during the 1994-1995 peso crisis. Mexico says the maximum amount it borrowed on the U.S. Treasury's emergency packet was $12.5 billion.
The amounts for the lastest repayments came from a wide variety of debt placements and other funds, including the recently placed 10-year global bond issue.
Banco de Mexico governor Miguel Mancera noted that, with the $1.5 billion prepayment to the International Monetary Fund, also announced on Wednesday, Mexico still owes the IMF $11.609 billion.

"We hope that, continuing the strategy we have adopted, that we can make new pre-payments that will allow the maturing debt concentrated in 1999 and 2000 to be reduced," Mancera said. In 1999 and 2000 alone, the central bank will have to pay off $8.985 billion to the IMF.
Mexico is also negotiating a new three-year precautionary loan program from the IMF to serve as a backup for future debt repayments.
On Wednesday, Ortiz said that loan would most likely be used for the heavy maturing debt schedule after 1998.

He said that it was possible they would not have to use the precuationary IMF loan, particularly if conditions in capital markets continue as they did last year and in the first two weeks of this year.
He said Mexico still did not have a final number for the size of the proposed IMF loan.
